## HTTP 103 Early Hints: Findings

### Three conclusions both sources support in common

**1. 103 is an informational status code that lets a server send header-field hints (primarily `Link`) before the final response, so clients can preload/preconnect early.**
- RFC 8297: "The 103 (Early Hints) informational status code indicates to the client that the server is likely to send a final response with the header fields included in the informational response" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)
- MDN: "The HTTP 103 Early Hints informational response may be sent by a server while it is still preparing a response, with hints about the sites and resources that the server expects the final response will link to. This allows a browser to preconnect to sites or start preloading resources" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/103)

**2. The `Link` header is the primary mechanism; it's used to convey preload/preconnect hints.**
- RFC 8297: "A client might recognize a Link header field value containing the relation type 'preload' and start fetching the target resource" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)
- MDN: "The early hint response is primarily intended for use with the Link header, which indicates the resources to be loaded," with examples using `Link: </style.css>; rel=preload; as=style` and `rel=preconnect` (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/103)

**3. Multiple 103 responses may be sent before the final response; they're merely hints and don't replace final-response headers.**
- RFC 8297: "As is the case with any informational response, a server might emit more than one 103 (Early Hints) response prior to sending a final response" and "these header fields only provide hints to the client; they do not replace the header fields on the final response" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)
- MDN: "A server might send multiple 103 responses, for example, following a redirect" and "Browsers only process the first early hints response" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/103)

### Two implementation / compatibility cautions

**1. HTTP/2-or-later limitation and handling of informational responses.** A client that mishandles an informational response over HTTP/1.1 can be a security/correctness risk, so the docs recommend restricting 103 to HTTP/2+ unless the client is known to handle informational responses correctly.
- RFC 8297: "an HTTP/1.1 client that mishandles an informational response as a final response is likely to consider all responses to the succeeding requests sent over the same connection to be part of the final response. Such behavior might constitute a cross-origin information disclosure vulnerability" and "a server might refrain from sending 103 (Early Hints) responses over HTTP/1.1 unless the client is known to handle informational responses correctly" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)
- MDN: "For compatibility and security reasons, it is recommended to only send HTTP 103 Early Hints responses over HTTP/2 or later unless the client is known to handle informational responses correctly. Most browsers limit support to HTTP/2 or later for this reason" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/103)

**2. Early-hint resources that are invalidated/overridden by the final response (including cross-origin redirects and CSP) are fetched but shouldn't be used.** Because hints are speculative, resources preloaded off a hint may prove wrong.
- RFC 8297: "there might be cases when this is not desirable, such as when the server learns that the header fields in the 103 (Early Hints) response are not correct before the final response is sent" — i.e., hints you acted on may not match the final response (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)

- RFC 8297: "The 103 (Early Hints) informational status code indicates to the client that the server is likely to send a final response with the header fields included in the informational response" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)
- MDN: "The HTTP 103 Early Hints informational response may be sent by a server while it is still preparing a response, with hints about the sites and resources that the server expects the final response will link to. This allows a browser to preconnect to sites or start preloading resources" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/103)

**2. The `Link` header is the primary mechanism; it's used to convey preload/preconnect hints.**
- RFC 8297: "A client might recognize a Link header field value containing the relation type 'preload' and start fetching the target resource" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)
- MDN: "The early hint response is primarily intended for use with the Link header, which indicates the resources to be loaded," with examples using `Link: </style.css>; rel=preload; as=style` and `rel=preconnect` (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/103)

**3. Multiple 103 responses may be sent before the final response; they're merely hints and don't replace final-response headers.**
- RFC 8297: "As is the case with any informational response, a server might emit more than one 103 (Early Hints) response prior to sending a final response" and "these header fields only provide hints to the client; they do not replace the header fields on the final response" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)
- MDN: "A server might send multiple 103 responses, for example, following a redirect" and "Browsers only process the first early hints response" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/103)

**1. HTTP/2-or-later limitation and handling of informational responses.** A client that mishandles an informational response over HTTP/1.1 can be a security/correctness risk, so the docs recommend restricting 103 to HTTP/2+ unless the client is known to handle informational responses correctly.
- RFC 8297: "an HTTP/1.1 client that mishandles an informational response as a final response is likely to consider all responses to the succeeding requests sent over the same connection to be part of the final response. Such behavior might constitute a cross-origin information disclosure vulnerability" and "a server might refrain from sending 103 (Early Hints) responses over HTTP/1.1 unless the client is known to handle informational responses correctly" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)
- MDN: "For compatibility and security reasons, it is recommended to only send HTTP 103 Early Hints responses over HTTP/2 or later unless the client is known to handle informational responses correctly. Most browsers limit support to HTTP/2 or later for this reason" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/103)

**2. Early-hint resources that are invalidated/overridden by the final response (including cross-origin redirects and CSP) are fetched but shouldn't be used.** Because hints are speculative, resources preloaded off a hint may prove wrong.
- RFC 8297: "there might be cases when this is not desirable, such as when the server learns that the header fields in the 103 (Early Hints) response are not correct before the final response is sent" — i.e., hints you acted on may not match the final response (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8297.html)
